paragraphs: One-sentence assessment | This career is worth exploring further only if you are willing to work with radiopharmaceuticals and patients daily, consistently complete dose checks, quality control and records according to procedures, and accept radiation protection and two-person review constraints.

Core output | Connect prescriptions and patient information, radiopharmaceutical preparation and dose records, imaging and quantitative results, and quality control and waste disposal records into a traceable examination file: images or data for physician interpretation, dose and timing records, and abnormality and adverse event reports, rather than just an image.

20—120-minute safe trial | Conduct an off-site exercise using a fictional prescription and patient information: create a checklist covering dose units, administration time, radionuclide and batch number, list three patient preparation items requiring confirmation before imaging and two abnormal conditions requiring suspension and escalation. Do not use this exercise to administer drugs, image or diagnose any real patient.

First hurdle | Verify authorization boundaries first: who may prescribe and adjust radiopharmaceuticals, review dose calculations and sign image interpretations. In the United States, authorized users oversee drug use and safety under NRC or Agreement State license conditions. In China, radiation workers must hold a Radiation Worker Certificate and undergo training and dose monitoring; medical institutions using radiopharmaceuticals must hold a Radiopharmaceutical Use License. Technologists must not replace physicians in diagnostic or treatment decisions.

Nuclear medicine technologists (O*NET-SOC 29-2033.00) prepare, administer and measure radioisotopes under physician direction for diagnosis, treatment and tracer research. They prepare radiopharmaceutical stock solutions under safety standards minimizing staff and patient radiation exposure; calculate, measure and record doses received, used and disposed of; operate gamma cameras, PET and other imaging equipment; process quantitative study data such as cardiac function; explain procedures and safety precautions to patients; perform equipment quality control; and store radiopharmaceuticals and dispose of radioactive waste under radiation safety procedures.

entries: Radiopharmaceutical preparation and administration | Prepare radiopharmaceuticals under physician direction and administer them according to safety standards, intravenously administering radiopharmaceuticals or radiation to detect or treat disease.
Dose calculation and records | Calculate, measure and record radiation doses or radiopharmaceuticals received, used and disposed of according to physicians' prescriptions.

Imaging and data processing | Use cameras to detect and map radiopharmaceutical distributions in the body, produce photographs or computer images, and use computers to process study data such as cardiac function.
Patient communication and assistance | Explain examination procedures and safety precautions, collect illness and medical history information, and assist patients during examinations.
Quality control and equipment maintenance | Perform quality control checks on laboratory equipment or cameras, and maintain and calibrate radioisotope and laboratory equipment.

Radiation safety and waste disposal | Dispose of radioactive materials and store radiopharmaceuticals according to radiation safety procedures, and train or supervise students and subordinate technologists.

paragraphs: Work takes place almost entirely in nuclear medicine departments and imaging centers within medical institutions. O*NET work context data show that 84% work indoors in controlled conditions daily, 89% use the telephone daily, and 91% maintain constant contact with others. Schedules are regular for 90%; 46% work 40 hours, 31% fewer than 40 hours, and 22% more than 40 hours per week.

Radiation and infection exposure are routine work conditions: O*NET reports that 100% face daily radiation exposure, 74% encounter disease or infections daily, 55% wear specialized protective equipment daily, and 62% wear common protective equipment daily. Meanwhile, 67% consider accuracy extremely important and 62% report extremely serious consequences of errors.

The emphasis is on traceable doses and procedures: aligning prescriptions, radionuclides and activity, administration times, patient preparation and imaging parameters, and suspending operations, reporting and following procedures when patient conditions or equipment are abnormal.

Quality is measured by consistent prescription and dose records, traceable administration and imaging times, equipment quality control completed at required intervals, complete interpretable images and data, compliant contamination and waste handling, and abnormalities and adverse events reported under procedures, rather than examination speed.

Responsibility boundaries | Training, Radiation Worker Certificates, practice qualifications, radiopharmaceutical use licensing and physician prescribing authority are distinct statuses. Technologists prepare and administer drugs, operate equipment and record results within their authorization. They must not independently increase doses, change prescriptions or replace physicians in diagnostic and treatment decisions. Specific operating permissions depend on institutional policies, license conditions and role authorization.

The workflow proceeds as follows: verify prescriptions and patient information → prepare radiopharmaceuticals and check doses → administer drugs and monitor patients → acquire images and data → process data and perform quality control → document reports and dispose of waste. Occupational boundaries | This occupation is distinct from radiologists, responsible for diagnostic and treatment decisions; radiation therapists, responsible for delivering external-beam treatment; and medical physicists, responsible for equipment and dosimetry systems. Prescribing, interpretation and dosimetry responsibilities belong to different professions.

Cardiovascular technologists and technicians | Mainly perform cardiovascular examinations, including electrocardiography and hemodynamic monitoring, focusing on cardiovascular signals and interventional assistance. This occupation centers on radiopharmaceuticals, nuclear medicine imaging and dose records, with different equipment and radiation safety requirements.

Clinical laboratory technologists and technicians | Mainly handle in vitro specimens and laboratory procedures, without authorization for radiopharmaceutical handling or nuclear medicine imaging. Working in the same medical institution does not imply shared radioactive material or imaging permissions.

Magnetic resonance imaging technologists | Center their work on MRI equipment and strong magnetic field safety. This occupation additionally handles radiopharmaceutical doses, contamination monitoring and waste control.

Adjacent roles may share patient communication, equipment quality control and recordkeeping skills, but education, licenses, certifications, radioactive material permissions and institutional authorization require renewed verification.
Compare the objects you want to handle over the long term: cardiovascular signals, in vitro specimens, magnetic resonance images, or radiopharmaceuticals and nuclear medicine images.

Centers on cardiovascular examinations and interventional assistance, with equipment and training pathways in cardiovascular technology, without radiopharmaceutical preparation, dose records or nuclear medicine imaging. This occupation's core outputs are interpretable nuclear medicine images and dose records.

Responsibility boundaries: tools may assist calculation and information organization but must not independently determine administered activity, change prescriptions, authorize examinations to proceed or diagnose. Authorized personnel verify and handle abnormalities according to medical orders and institutional procedures.

Human control points (editorial synthesis): verify the patient, prescription, activity, timing and equipment status. Reviewer numbers and signature requirements follow institutional policies; the two-person review recommended on this page cannot be extended into a uniform requirement of the cited regulations.

Data requirements (editorial recommendation): real patient identities, images and dose records must follow institutional data policies and applicable privacy rules; synthetic teaching data may be analyzed separately. The FDA device list supports device authorization checks but does not establish that every text organization tool requires medical device approval.

Capability development | Build skills in radiopharmaceuticals and dose calculations, imaging equipment operation and quality control, patient communication and monitoring, radiation protection and contamination response, and collaboration with physicians and medical physicists, beyond producing images faster.

The 2025 BLS OEWS data displayed by O*NET report the exact occupation 29-2033.00: median hourly wage of USD 48.74 and median annual wage of USD 101,370. These figures are not starting salaries or individual quoted rates.

OEWS excludes self-employment income. Wages include commissions, incentive pay and production bonuses, while excluding overtime premiums, shift differentials and nonproduction bonuses, among other items. Performance bonuses cannot be categorically excluded, and the figures are not individual take-home income.
Lower percentiles are not starting salaries for new graduates, and distribution data cannot be used to estimate individual take-home pay or after-tax income.

Scheduling, on-call and performance pay structures differ among hospitals, outpatient imaging centers and specialty institutions. Verify the specific employer, region and role responsibilities. US figures cannot be converted into individual income in mainland China.

Verification method | Personality and interest labels cannot determine fit. Use a fictional prescription to practice dose and patient preparation checks, and obtain evaluation from qualified personnel in a teaching or guided training setting.

This checklist highlights risks and does not replace institutional radiation protection, medical orders or role policies. Chinese medical institutions using radiopharmaceuticals must meet safety protection, premises, equipment, sanitary environment and storage requirements. Use of compounded radiopharmaceutical preparations requires the corresponding grade of Radiopharmaceutical Use License. Category one and two use licenses were canceled from January 20, 2025; not all drug use can be treated as requiring this license. Personnel checks, quality control, dose and contamination monitoring, waste handoffs and authorization scope must still be implemented separately.

Risks center on identity–prescription mismatches, activity or timing deviations, missing quality control, contamination and waste handling, protection and monitoring omissions, and unauthorized operations. Verify, review, document and escalate under institutional procedures; two-person review follows applicable policies.

Among US O*NET respondents, 100% report daily radiation exposure, 74% daily infection exposure, 67% consider accuracy extremely important, and 62% report extremely serious error consequences. These are not injury probabilities. Verify Chinese training and monitoring against health authority rules and drug use against the 2024 revised measures and 2025 licensing reform.

Relevant roles include administration, activity records, equipment quality control, patient assistance and waste handoffs, as well as collaborating physicians, medical physicists and protection personnel. New employees should develop checking habits under guidance; this review has no evidence comparing their error probabilities with those of others.

Possible consequences | Verification or dose errors may cause abnormal patient exposure and treatment deviations. Missing quality control may lead to misdiagnosis or repeat examinations. Improper contamination and waste handling may contaminate the environment and personnel. Excessive personal doses may cause occupational health harm and legal liability.

Role sample (editorial synthesis, not a job advertisement): a common US entry route is accredited nuclear medicine technology education and clinical training. Certification is common; verify licenses by state and role. Work includes administering drugs under medical orders, imaging, quality control and patient assistance, with nights, weekends and on-call work in some roles. Chinese role conditions require separate verification of local staffing, training, licensing and authorization.

paragraphs: Boundary note one | Education completion, professional certification, state licensure, Radiation Worker Certificates and institutional role authorization are distinct statuses. No certificate automatically confers permission to operate specific equipment or administer drugs.

Boundary note two: Chinese medical institutions using radiopharmaceuticals must meet safety protection, premises, equipment, sanitary environment and storage requirements. Use of compounded radiopharmaceutical preparations requires the corresponding grade of Radiopharmaceutical Use License. Category one and two use licenses were canceled from January 20, 2025; not all drug use can be treated as requiring this license. US medical radioactive material use follows NRC or Agreement State licensing. Technologists performing tasks should receive appropriate training and authorized-user supervision.

Boundary note three | Radiation protection and dose monitoring are ongoing obligations. Pre-work training, regular in-service training, personal dose monitoring and health examinations must follow policies and be documented.

Boundary note four | Technologists do not bear physicians' diagnostic or prescribing responsibilities. Drug administration, imaging and records follow prescriptions; physicians make interpretive conclusions and treatment decisions.

Editorial development recommendation: after supervised learning, undertake routine examinations within medical orders, applicable supervision and institutional authorization, then develop quantitative examination, teaching and quality control skills. Verify certification and licensing requirements by jurisdiction, role and employer; no uniform duration or automatic advancement is established.

locale_requirements.credential_boundary: Verify education, professional certification, applicable state licenses, radiation worker conditions, institutional licensing and role authorization separately. Certificates do not automatically confer equipment, prescribing or interpretation permissions.
locale_requirements.jurisdiction: Occupational facts on this page use the US O*NET 29-2033.00 definition. US licensing and certification references include state regulators and O*NET certification lists; radioactive material use refers to the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) licensing framework. Chinese qualifications, training and dose monitoring refer to the Measures for Occupational Health Management of Radiation Workers; radiopharmaceutical use refers to the Measures for the Administration of Radiopharmaceuticals; and radiological diagnosis and treatment protection refers to the Provisions on the Administration of Radiological Diagnosis and Treatment. Current regulations for other jurisdictions and institutions require separate verification.
locale_requirements.summary: Most US nuclear medicine technologists hold professional certification, and some states require licensure. Verify mandatory certification, licenses and specialty credentials against the target state and employer. Chinese medical institutions using radiopharmaceuticals must meet safety protection, premises, equipment, sanitary environment and storage requirements. Use of compounded radiopharmaceutical preparations requires the corresponding grade of Radiopharmaceutical Use License. Category one and two use licenses were canceled from January 20, 2025; not all drug use can be treated as requiring this license. O*NET's education survey of 63% two-year degrees, 22% bachelor's degrees and 6% postbaccalaureate certificates applies only to US respondents.

components.definition_block: Nuclear medicine technologists (O*NET-SOC 29-2033.00) prepare, administer and measure radioisotopes under physician direction for treatment, diagnosis and tracer research: preparing radiopharmaceuticals under safety standards minimizing radiation exposure; calculating and recording doses received, used and disposed of; operating imaging equipment to acquire and generate images; processing quantitative data such as cardiac function; explaining procedures and assisting patients; performing equipment quality control; and storing drugs and disposing of radioactive waste under radiation safety procedures. Actual permitted activities depend on relevant education, target state and employer requirements, applicable license conditions and institutional role authorization.
